en: Itivuttaka 91: Tikanipāta, Pañcamavagga (The Fifth Chapter) Thus it was said by the Blessed One; having thus spoken, the Well-Farer [proceeded] further, saying: "Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a stone pillar, the person who is like a tree stump, and the person who is like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a stone pillar? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions. This, monks, is called a person like a stone pillar. And how, monks, is one a person like a tree stump? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions. But when he is reproved by others, he becomes angry, harbors resentment, and speaks words of harshness. This, monks, is called a person like a tree stump. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions. But when he is reproved by others, he does not become angry, harbor resentment, or speak words of harshness. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus flower. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. The Discourse on Livelihood.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard:
"Bhikkhus, this is the lowest of livelihoods, namely, living as a beggar."
“Monks, this is a reproach in the world: ‘You wander about with a bowl in hand like a beggar.
Yet, monks, it is for the sake of a purpose, and depending on a purpose, that sons of good family enter upon this life;
they do so neither driven by kings, nor driven by thieves, nor oppressed by debt, nor oppressed by fear, nor constrained by the need for a livelihood.”

Moreover, monks, this clansman has gone forth thinking: "We are immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; we are immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.
Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.
It is for this reason, monks, that this clansman has gone forth.

"And yet he is covetous for sensual pleasures, with intense lust, malevolent in mind, with corrupt intentions, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind,

and with unrestrained faculties. Just as a torch of hay, burning at both ends and smeared with excrement in the middle, serves neither as firewood in the village nor as fuel in the forest— just so, monks,
I say this person has fallen away from the enjoyments of a householder and does not fulfill the goal of recluseship."
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“Falling away from the enjoyments of a householder...”
And the goal of recluseship is ill-fated for him;
being consumed, he scatters [his remains] and perishes like a funeral torch.
Many with saffron robes around their necks,
evil-natured and unrestrained,
are wicked because of their wicked deeds.
They are reborn in hell.
Better it would be to swallow a glowing iron ball,
heated like a crest of flame, than that.
"And whatever an immoral person, unrestrained, might eat as alms from the kingdom"—
this matter too was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The second.
